rationale: Mordecai's dream opens with voices, thunder and an earthquake, before its nations prepare to attack the righteous people. Isaiah joins thunder, earthquake and a great sound in the Lord's visitation, then likens the nations attacking Jerusalem to people dreaming. The shared cluster of tumult, threatened people and dream imagery supports a literary comparison; it does not identify the dream's events with Isaiah's siege or import Isaiah's fire into Esther.
source_text: This was his dream: Look! Voices and tumult, thunders and an earthquake, disturbance upon the earth!

target_units.text: from the Lord Sabaoth. For there will be a visitation with thunder, earthquake and a great sound, a rushing storm and a consuming flame of fire.
Like someone dreaming in sleep will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Ariel, all who marched against Jerusalem, and all assembled against her and afflicting her.

They will be like people drinking and eating in sleep; when they rise, their dream is futile. As a thirsty person dreams of drinking but wakes still thirsty, his soul having hoped in vain, so will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Mount Zion.

relationship: shared imagery of a dark day of distress
rationale: The dream announces a day of darkness and gloom amid the righteous nation's fear of destruction. Joel announces the near day of the Lord as darkness and gloom with turmoil and an approaching force. Both use the same dark-day imagery for overwhelming peril, while Esther's dream and Joel's announcement retain their own settings and are not treated as predictions of one event.
source_text: Look! A day of darkness and gloom, affliction and distress, suffering and great disturbance upon the earth!

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Proclaim on My holy mountain, and let all who inhabit the land be thrown into turmoil, because the Lord’s day is present; it is near,

a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist. Like dawn a numerous and strong people will be poured over the mountains. Its like has never existed, nor will another follow it through the years, for generations upon generations.

relationship: shared language of darkness and affliction
rationale: Esther's dream calls the coming ordeal a day of darkness, gloom, affliction and distress. Zephaniah similarly accumulates darkness, gloom, affliction and constraint in describing the Lord's day. The dense shared description expresses overwhelming calamity; Zephaniah explicitly names divine wrath against sin, which is not transferred to Esther's threatened righteous nation.
source_text: Look! A day of darkness and gloom, affliction and distress, suffering and great disturbance upon the earth!

target_units.text: For the Lord’s great day is near, near and very swift. The sound of the Lord’s day is bitter and harsh; it is appointed mighty.
That day is a day of wrath, a day of affliction and constraint, a day of untimely ruin and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist,
a day of trumpet and shouting against fortified cities and high corners.
I will press people hard, and they will walk like the blind because they sinned against the Lord. He will pour out their blood like dust and their flesh like dung.

relationship: prayer grounded in remembrance of the Lord's works
rationale: Mordecai implores the Lord while remembering all His works; the following prayer invokes creation and the redemption of Israel from Egypt. The psalm remembers the Lord's works, meditates on all His deeds, and recalls His redemption of the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Both ground an appeal in remembered divine action, without making Mordecai the psalm's speaker or claiming a quotation.
source_text: and he implored the Lord, remembering all the Lord’s works, and said:

target_units.text: I remembered the Lord’s works, for I will remember Thy wonders from the beginning,
and meditate on all Thy works, and speak at length about Thy practices.
God, Thy way is in the Holy One; what god is great like our God?
Thou art the God who does wonders; Thou madest Thy power known among the peoples.
With Thine arm Thou didst redeem Thy people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Diapsalma.

relationship: contrast between mortal royal praise and God's glory
rationale: Esther fears that nations will praise worthless things and admire a king of flesh for ever, in a prayer defending the praise and glory owed to the Lord. Acts depicts a royal audience acclaiming Herod's speech as a god's voice rather than a human being's, followed by his death for failing to give glory to God. The comparison concerns misplaced exaltation of a mortal ruler, not an identification of Herod with Esther's king or of the two occasions.
source_text: and to open the mouth of nations to praise worthless things, and that a king of flesh might be admired for ever.

target_units.text: On an appointed day Herod put on royal clothing, sat on the tribunal, and delivered an address to them.
The populace shouted, “A god’s voice, and not a human being’s!”
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him because he did not give the glory to God. He was eaten by worms and breathed his last.

rationale: Esther asks the Lord to rescue the people and help her, describing herself as alone with no one except Him. The psalmist asks for mercy because he is alone and poor, then seeks rescue from distress and multiplying enemies. Both join confessed isolation to a direct plea for the Lord's protection; the psalm's poverty and requested forgiveness are not added to Esther's words.
source_text: But rescue us by Thy hand, and help me, who am alone and have no one except Thee, Lord.

target_units.text: Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor.
The afflictions of my heart widened; bring me out of my distresses.
See my humiliation and my toil, and forgive all my sins.
See my enemies, for they multiplied and hated me with unjust hatred.
Guard my soul and rescue me; may I not be put to shame, for I hoped in Thee.

relationship: rejection of supposed escape from God's scrutiny
rationale: The royal letter condemns the arrogant supposition that people can escape the justice of God who watches everything. The psalm answers wrongdoers who say that the Lord will not see or understand: the Maker of eyes perceives, disciplines nations and knows human reasoning. Both expose imagined impunity as incompatible with God's perception and judgment, without identifying the psalm's offenders with the letter's subjects.
source_text: They not only abolish gratitude among people, but, lifted up by the boasts of those unacquainted with goodness, they suppose they will escape the evil-hating justice of God, Who always watches over all things.

target_units.text: They said, The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.
Understand now, you senseless among the people; and you fools, become wise at last.
Does the One who planted the ear not hear, or the One who formed the eye not perceive?
Will the One who disciplines nations not rebuke— the One who teaches humankind knowledge?
The Lord knows human reasonings, that they are futile.

relationship: rejection of imagined concealment from God
rationale: Esther's letter rejects the thought that the arrogant can evade God's justice while He watches all things. Sirach forbids saying that one will be hidden from the Lord among the multitude and the vast creation, recalls the terror of His visitation, and calls such reasoning foolish. Both challenge presumed escape from divine notice; Sirach's imagined excuse of smallness is distinguished from the letter's arrogance and ingratitude.
source_text: They not only abolish gratitude among people, but, lifted up by the boasts of those unacquainted with goodness, they suppose they will escape the evil-hating justice of God, Who always watches over all things.

target_units.text: Do not say, “I will be hidden from the Lord; who will remember me from on high? Among a numerous people I will certainly not be known, for what is my soul in the immeasurable creation?”
Behold, heaven and the heaven of heaven, the abyss and the earth will be shaken at His visitation.
Together the mountains and the foundations of the earth are shaken with trembling when He looks upon them.
Yet no heart will consider these things, and who will ponder His ways?
There is also a tempest that a person will not see, and most of His works are hidden.
Who will announce works of righteousness? Who will wait? For the covenant is far away.
Someone deficient in heart thinks these things; a foolish and wandering man thinks foolish things.
